source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) The Extended Mind
finding: Proposes active externalism: external parts of the world coupled with an organism in the here and now can be parts of the cognitive process. The core argument is the parity principle.
numbers: Philosophical argument; no data.
quote: If, as we confront some task, a part of the world functions as a process which, were it done in the head, we would have no hesitation
limits: Argument by intuition and functional role; critics dispute that parity is a good test.
agent_relevance: The notebook, the scratch file and the code interpreter are parts of the thinker if they play the right role. Design them as cognitive parts, not as add-ons.

source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) Otto and Inga case
finding: Otto has Alzheimer's disease and keeps the museum address in a notebook. Inga recalls it from memory. Both walk to 53rd Street. The notebook plays the same role as Inga's memory, so Otto believed the address before he looked. Twin Otto, whose notebook says 51st Street, shows that belief can differ when the insides of the skin are identical.
numbers: Single thought experiment: MoMA on 53rd Street; Twin Otto notebook says 51st Street.
limits: Thought experiment, not tested on people. Depends on what counts as a belief.
agent_relevance: A stored note counts as the agent's own standing knowledge only if it is used the way memory is used. Gives a test for which notes to treat as the agent's belief state.

source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) Coupling conditions
finding: Conditions for a resource to count as part of belief: constancy (reliably used), availability (directly accessible), automatic endorsement (retrieved content is trusted without checking), and past conscious endorsement (the authors call this one debatable). Social cases (spouse, secretary) are allowed, and the criteria come in degrees.
numbers: Four criteria; the first three carry the main weight.
quote: the relevant external features are active, playing a crucial role in the here-and-now
limits: Criteria are graded, not sharp. Automatic endorsement is the one most at odds with a safe agent.
agent_relevance: Conflicts with our guardrails: automatic endorsement of retrieved notes is exactly the failure G2/G3 guard against. Endorse a note only after a code-checked pass, so notes are extended memory with an audit step.

source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) epistemic action and Tetris
finding: The paper cites Kirsh and Maglio: Tetris players rotate shapes on screen to see if they fit instead of rotating them in the head. These are epistemic actions: actions that change the world to help recognition and search.
numbers: No numbers in this paper; numbers are in Kirsh and Maglio (1994), see below.
quote: Epistemic actions alter the world so as to aid and augment cognitive processes such as recognition and search.
limits: Secondary use of the Tetris data.
agent_relevance: Writing intermediate results, running code or drawing a diagram is thinking, not output. Count such steps as part of the reasoning trace.

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action: Tetris keystroke data
finding: In Tetris, players rotate and translate zoids almost from the moment a zoid appears, before any plan could be finished. A classical plan-then-act model (their RoboTetris) cannot explain this. They explain it as epistemic action: acting to compute.
numbers: Rotation begins in earnest 400-600 ms after a zoid appears. Shortest time between keystrokes is about 75 ms; mean about 250 ms. Only 4 actions exist: left, right, rotate, drop.
limits: A video game with fully determinate effects. Authors say the strategy pays off because there are no hidden states or other agents.
agent_relevance: Acting early to see what happens can beat planning first, when actions are cheap, reversible and deterministic. Fits cheap code execution in a sandbox; does not fit costly or irreversible actions.

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) mental vs physical rotation timing
finding: A Shepard-Metzler style test with Tetris players shows mental rotation is much slower than pressing the rotate key. Reaction time rises linearly with angle difference. Physical rotation also avoids the attention and memory costs of holding an image.
numbers: Physical 90-degree rotation can take about 100 ms; mental rotation of a zoid 90 degrees is estimated at 800-1200 ms. Three players only (intermediate, advanced, expert), 8 presentations per pair. Even adding 200 ms for choosing the key, the gap stays large.
limits: Tiny pilot sample; the 800-1200 ms figure is an estimate from pilot data.
agent_relevance: A tool call that costs a tenth of the internal computation is worth making. Give the agent a rule for when to prefer a tool call over a long internal chain.

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) epistemic functions and cost-benefit model
finding: Rotations serve epistemic roles: speed up shape identification, make matching to the contour easier, and cut unreliable computation. Translating to the wall and back checks column position and is used more often when the drop is higher. Authors sketch a cost-benefit model: the chance of an epistemic action grows with how informative it is.
numbers: Verification routine (translate to nearest wall and back) happens in a small percentage of drops and rises with drop height (Figure 15). A full shape takes about half a second to emerge (about 150 ms per row).
limits: Cost-benefit model is qualitative. Authors note that planning needs a redefined state space that includes epistemic moves.
agent_relevance: The agent's planner should include look actions (run, print, test) in its action set and price them. Design hint for operator choice in the schema.

source: Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011) Google effects on memory, Experiment 1 (modified Stroop)
finding: After hard trivia questions, people were slower to name the ink colour of computer words than of general words. The authors read this as computers being primed when we do not know an answer.
numbers: After hard questions: computer words 712 ms (SD 413) vs general words 591 ms (SD 204), t(68)=3.26, p<.003 (N=69). After easy questions: 603 vs 559 ms, t(68)=2.98. Search-engine brands after hard questions 818 ms (SD 517) vs general brands 614 ms; interaction F(1,66)=5.02, p<.03.
limits: Small N (69); large SDs; the paper was one of the 21 studies in Camerer et al. (2018) (see below). Stroop interference is an indirect measure.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that a knowledge gap pulls toward the tool. Do not build on this effect.

source: Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011) Experiment 2 (believed saved vs erased)
finding: People who believed typed trivia statements would be erased recalled more than people who believed they would be saved. Explicit instructions to remember made no difference.
numbers: Recall: erase 0.31 (SD .04), erase+remember 0.29, save 0.22, save+remember 0.19. Omnibus F(3,56)=2.80, p<.05. 40 statements; 2x2 between subjects, N about 60.
limits: Small cells (about 15 each); only the omnibus test was reported as significant.
agent_relevance: Belief that a store exists lowers the effort to retain. For the agent: an external note may reduce internal encoding in the same context, so the schema should say which facts must live in the prompt.

source: Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011) Experiments 3 and 4 (what vs where)
finding: People remember where information is saved better than what it was, when they expect to look it up.
numbers: Exp 4 (N about 33): recall of folder location M=0.49 (SD .26) vs recall of the statement M=0.23 (SD .14), t(31)=6.70, p<.001. Exp 3: statements believed erased had best recognition (0.93, SD .09) while accuracy for saved/erased status was 0.61 and 0.66 for saved items.
limits: Folder names were generic (FACTS etc.) and few; lab typing task, not real web search.
agent_relevance: Index over content: the agent should keep pointers (where) in context and full text in the store. Matches retrieval notes with short keys.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science (includes Sparrow et al. 2011)
finding: 21 social-science studies from Nature and Science 2010-2015 were replicated with pre-registered, high-powered designs. 13 (62%) replicated, and effect sizes were about 50% of the original. Sparrow et al. (2011) was one of the 21. The text I opened says only that its authors gave no materials or feedback and later noted design differences.
numbers: 21 studies; 13 (62%) replicated; mean replication effect about 50% of original; replication samples about 5 times larger; estimated true-positive rate 67%; relative effect size of true positives 71%.
limits: Per-study outcome and numbers for Sparrow sit in the supplement, which I did not open. From memory the Sparrow replication is counted among the failures; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Treat the Google-effect literature as shaky at the single-study level; original effect sizes are probably inflated.

source: Gong and Yang (2024) Google effects on memory: a meta-analytical review
finding: Random-effects meta-analysis of 22 articles (35 comparisons, N=30,889, ages 12-89) finds a moderate significant effect of internet reliance on cognition; subgroups differ. Region moderates the effect; year, age, sex and sample size do not.
numbers: Subgroup d [95% CI]: cognitive load 0.73 [0.22,1.24]; behavioural phenotype 0.39 [0.16,0.61]; cognitive self-esteem 0.91 [0.23,1.59]; cognitive measurement 0.56 [-0.15,1.28] (ns); psychophysiology 1.01 [-0.12,2.13] (ns). Region moderator Q=6.20, p<.05, 13.18% of heterogeneity.
limits: Broad mixed outcome categories; publication bias judged by funnel plot by eye only; pooled d and I2 not in the text I read; does not itself replicate Sparrow. I read it through a page summariser.
agent_relevance: Overall direction supports costs of reliance, but the measured constructs are loose. Use for context only.

source: Boldt and Gilbert (2019) Confidence guides spontaneous cognitive offloading
finding: In a delayed-intention task, people set external reminders more when less confident in their memory, whether or not the reminder strategy was explained. Offloading improved hit rates. Offloading is steered by metacognitive confidence.
numbers: 435 recruited, 363 analysed. Mean hit rate 85.4% (instructed 87.2%, spontaneous 83.8%, group difference F(1,361)=1.8, p=.18). Phase 2 (reminders allowed) 88.1% vs Phase 1 82.7%, F(1,361)=39.1, p<.001. People were underconfident overall.
limits: MTurk online task with 10 circles; reminders are cheap; short laboratory setting.
agent_relevance: Offload on a confidence signal, as G1 says (act on a signal, not on a schedule). The agent should write notes when its own check says it may forget, not at fixed times.

source: Ward, Duke, Gneezy and Bos (2017) Brain drain (as reported by Skowronek et al. 2023)
finding: Original claim: the mere presence of one's own smartphone uses cognitive capacity. Only location mattered (desk, pocket or bag, other room), not whether the phone was on. Effects were strongest for high-dependence users.
numbers: Numbers for the original were not read; this entry is from a secondary text.
limits: Original paper not opened. Secondary description only. Thornton et al. found harm only for high-demand tasks.
agent_relevance: A possible attention cost of an always-near tool. Weak evidence; see the failed replication next.

source: Ruiz Pardo and Minda (2022) Reexamining the brain drain effect (as reported by Skowronek et al. 2023)
finding: Used the tasks of Ward et al.'s second experiment and found no difference between phone locations (on desk, in pocket or bag, other room) on operation span or go/no-go.
numbers: No numbers recorded in the text read. Result: no location effect on either task.
limits: Described secondhand. Hartmann et al. also found no overall effect on short-term and prospective memory, except in low-dependence users.
agent_relevance: A failed replication of the strongest 'tool presence costs attention' claim. Do not add attention-cost guardrails for tool presence.

source: Skowronek, Seifert and Lindberg (2023) The mere presence of a smartphone reduces basal attentional performance
finding: A small study found lower attention with a switched-off smartphone present than without. Authors note mixed prior results and moderators (dependence, task demand).
numbers: N=42 (21 per group). Attention performance 108.95 without vs 99.71 with phone: F(1,40)=6.168, p=.017, eta2=.134. Speed 108.57 vs 98.48: F(1,40)=7.592, p=.009, eta2=.160.
limits: Very small sample; 93% White, highly educated; one attention test; the same literature includes null replications.
agent_relevance: Keep as a weak, inconsistent result. Shows that tool-in-the-room effects are fragile.

source: Risko and Gilbert (2016) Cognitive offloading
finding: Defines cognitive offloading as using physical action to reduce the mental demand of a task, and reviews when and why people offload and how it is controlled. Not opened this session; the definition is as quoted in Boldt and Gilbert (2019).
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened. Use only as a pointer.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary for the agent: offloading is a decision under uncertainty about one's own memory and ability.

source: Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023): tools as learned self-supervised extension
finding: A 6.7B GPT-J model is fine-tuned to decide for itself when to call a calculator, QA system, search engines, a translator or a calendar. In zero-shot tests it beats much larger models on facts and arithmetic.
numbers: LAMA SQuAD/Google-RE/T-REx: Toolformer 33.8/11.5/53.5 vs GPT-3 175B 26.8/7.0/39.8, OPT 66B 21.6/2.9/30.1, GPT-J 17.8/4.9/31.9. Math ASDiv/SVAMP/MAWPS: Toolformer 40.4/29.4/44.0 vs GPT-3 14.8/6.3/15.0, GPT-J 7.5/5.2/9.9. Calculator used for 97.9% of math examples.
limits: Table values read from a column-merged text extraction; at most one API call per input; no chaining; no tool cost model. Still behind GPT-3 175B on QA with the Wikipedia tool.
agent_relevance: Tools extend a small model past a large one on lookups and sums. Supports using code or search for facts and arithmetic instead of free recall.

source: Toolformer scaling of tool use
finding: The ability to use tools only emerges at around 775M parameters in the GPT-2 family. Smaller models do the same with and without tools, except for the easy Wikipedia search.
numbers: Tested at 124M, 355M, 775M and 1.6B parameters, with three tools. A large gap between with-tool and without-tool remains at the biggest size. Calendar tool used for 54.8% of DATESET examples.
limits: Single model family and training recipe; later models are far beyond these sizes.
agent_relevance: Coupling needs competence on the thinker's side. A weak model cannot use an external store well, so match the notes interface to model size.

source: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) interleaving thought and action: HotpotQA and FEVER
finding: With PaLM-540B, interleaving reasoning with Wikipedia lookups cuts hallucination. ReAct beats chain of thought on FEVER but not on HotpotQA. The best results come from mixing ReAct with self-consistency.
numbers: HotpotQA EM: CoT 29.4 vs ReAct 27.4; best ReAct->CoT-SC 35.1 (Standard 28.7 vs CoT 29.4 in the table text, with column order unclear). FEVER acc: CoT 56.3, ReAct 60.9, best CoT-SC->ReAct 64.6. ReAct+CoT-SC matches CoT-SC at 21 samples using 3-5 samples.
limits: Table columns merged in my extraction; the text states ReAct 27.4 vs CoT 29.4 on HotpotQA and 60.9 vs 56.3 on FEVER. Few-shot prompts, one model family.
agent_relevance: Grounding in a store has a price: flexibility. Back off to an ungrounded path when the grounded path fails, chosen by a code check.

source: ReAct error analysis on HotpotQA
finding: Hand labelling of 200 trajectories shows chain of thought fails mostly by hallucination, ReAct by reasoning loops and uninformative search.
numbers: False-positive rate from hallucination: CoT 14% vs ReAct 6%; hallucination is 56% of CoT failures. Uninformative search is 23% of ReAct error cases. ReAct often repeats its previous thought and action.
limits: 50 correct and 50 incorrect per method; labelled by the authors.
agent_relevance: Add a loop detector (repeat of thought plus action) to the impasse detector as a code-checked signal.

source: ReAct on ALFWorld and WebShop
finding: In interactive environments, adding thoughts to actions raises success over action-only and over trained imitation and RL agents.
numbers: ALFWorld best ReAct trial 71% vs best Act 45% vs best BUTLER 37%; worst ReAct trial 48%; ReAct beats Act by 33-90% relative (mean 62%) over six trials. WebShop success 40.0 (score 66.6) vs Act 30.1, IL 29.1, IL+RL 28.7; expert human 59.6.
limits: Prompting with 1-2 examples; best-of-6 trial reporting on ALFWorld; far from human experts on WebShop.
agent_relevance: Thinking alongside acting is a better coupling than acting alone. Supports alternating thought and action steps.

source: Packer et al. (2023) MemGPT: operating-system style memory tiers
finding: Gives the model an in-context main memory plus external archival and recall storage that it edits with function calls, with interrupts for control flow. This is Otto's notebook built as software.
limits: Benchmark built by the authors from Multi-Session Chat; baselines are fixed-context truncation, not other memory systems.
agent_relevance: Direct support for external notes as a managed tier. Test our notes layer on our own retrieval benchmark before relying on it.

source: MemGPT nested key-value retrieval
finding: Fixed-context models collapse on multi-hop lookups, while a model that can query external storage repeatedly does not.
numbers: Nested KV with 140 UUID pairs (about 8k tokens), 0 to 4 nesting levels, 30 orderings each: GPT-3.5 hits 0% accuracy at 1 level, GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo hit 0% by 3 levels; MemGPT with GPT-4 is unaffected by nesting level.
limits: Synthetic task.
agent_relevance: Repeated external queries solve multi-hop lookups that in-context reasoning fails. Use code-driven lookup loops.

source: Graves, Wayne and Danihelka (2014) Neural Turing Machines
finding: Early formal model of a network coupled to an addressable external memory by differentiable read and write heads. A computational reading of extended mind.
numbers: Trained on copy sequences up to length 20; NTM copies length 100 and 120 sequences with no further training while LSTM degrades beyond length 20. NTM learns faster and to lower cost than LSTM on copy.
limits: Toy algorithmic tasks; small memories; hard to train.
agent_relevance: The value of an external store comes from learning an algorithm over it that generalises in length, not from the store alone. For us, code is the algorithm over the store.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT: cognitive debt in essay writing
finding: Three groups (LLM, search engine, brain only) wrote essays over three sessions with EEG. LLM users showed weaker connectivity, lower ownership and poorer recall of their own text. The authors call this cognitive debt.
numbers: N=54 (18 per group; 55 completed). Session 1 failure to quote own essay: 83.3% (15/18) in the LLM group vs 11.1% (2/18) in search and brain-only; 0/18 LLM participants gave a correct quote in session 1. Session 4 had 18 participants and no search group.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed; small sample; essay task; EEG interpretation contested.
agent_relevance: Extension through an LLM may reduce encoding and ownership, so the where-not-what pattern may be stronger with LLMs. For our agent: a note it only copies in may not be understood; require it to restate and test.

source: Hutchins (1995) Cognition in the Wild
finding: Ethnography of ship navigation: the navigation team and its instruments compute together, so the unit of analysis for cognition is the team plus artifacts. This founded distributed cognition.
numbers: No numbers recorded; book not opened.
limits: Not opened this session; description from background knowledge. Verify before relying on it.
agent_relevance: Supports modelling the agent plus its tools and notes as one system with a division of labour.

source: Wegner (1987) Transactive memory
finding: Couples and groups divide memory labour, each knowing what the other knows, using a shared directory. Sparrow et al. (2011) extend this to computers, as stated in their paper.
numbers: No numbers recorded; not opened.
limits: Not opened this session; check before quoting.
agent_relevance: A directory of what each store or tool knows is the key object; give the agent such a directory.

source: Adams and Aizawa (2001) The bounds of cognition; Rupert (2004) Challenges to the hypothesis of extended cognition
finding: Main critics of the extended mind. Adams and Aizawa: the coupling-constitution fallacy and the claim that cognition needs intrinsic non-derived content. Rupert: extended memory differs in its properties from biological memory, so it is not the same kind.
numbers: No numbers recorded; not opened.
limits: Not opened this session; summary from background knowledge. Verify.
agent_relevance: Even if notes are not mind, they work as memory in practice. Keep the engineering claim modest: functional role plus audit.
